The Higgs boson. An elementary particle in the Standard Model of particle physics, the quantized excitation of the Higgs field, an energy field thought to permeate all of space. Its existence explains how other fundamental particles acquire mass. Particles that interact strongly with the Higgs field behave as though they are heavier, while those that do not, like the photon, remain massless. This mechanism was proposed in nineteen sixty-four, most famously by Peter Higgs alongside François Englert and Robert Brout, and several others including Guralnik, Hagen, and Kibble.

The Higgs is a scalar boson with spin zero, the only fundamental scalar particle in the Standard Model. It was discovered in twenty twelve by the ATLAS and CMS experiments at CERN's Large Hadron Collider near Geneva. Its mass is about one hundred twenty-five GeV per c squared, roughly one hundred thirty-three times the mass of a proton. The discovery was so significant that the twenty thirteen Nobel Prize in Physics went to Peter Higgs and François Englert the year after confirmation.

It is popularly called the God particle, a name from Leon Lederman's book that physicists generally dislike. The nickname is misleading and has become something of a running joke in the physics community. The Higgs completed the Standard Model, the most successful theory of fundamental forces and particles, by supplying the long-sought mechanism for mass without breaking the theory's symmetries. Its discovery was one of the largest scientific collaborations in history and a triumph of the LHC, the world's biggest machine. Open questions remain about whether the Higgs is truly elementary, why its mass is what it is—the hierarchy problem—and how it connects to dark matter and physics beyond the Standard Model, keeping it central to ongoing research.
